author: The Infographics Show
description:
For decades, Canada sent roughly 70 cents of every military procurement dollar to U.S. defense companies. Now it wants out.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced plans to redirect much more defense spending toward Canadian companies, reducing a dependency built over generations. But breaking away from America is far harder than changing where the contracts go.
Canada relies on U.S.-made weapons, aircraft, missile systems, GPS infrastructure, and deeply integrated supply chains. Even many “Canadian” defense companies are owned by American firms. And Canada isn’t alone.
European countries are also steering more military spending toward domestic suppliers as confidence in U.S. security guarantees weakens.

American defense dominance won’t disappear overnight, but the system that supported it for decades is beginning to change.

00:35 - How Canada Became Economically Dependent on the U.S.
02:09 - The Trade Talks That Triggered an Economic Divorce
03:47 - How the U.S.-Canada Tariff War
title: 70 Cents of Every Dollar Is Over: The Collapse of American Defense Dominance

description:
Tesamorelin is being promoted as a peptide that can target the dangerous visceral fat surrounding your organs, but how does it actually work?

Unlike traditional weight-loss drugs, Tesamorelin doesn’t directly suppress appetite or simply burn calories. It mimics Growth Hormone-Releasing Hormone, or GHRH, signaling the pituitary gland to increase the body’s own natural pulses of growth hormone. That matters because visceral fat appears particularly sensitive to growth hormone signaling.
Tesamorelin was originally developed to treat HIV-associated lipodystrophy, a condition that can cause dangerous abdominal fat accumulation in people receiving antiretroviral therapy. In 2010, the FDA approved it under the brand name Egrifta. Clinical trials found that Tesamorelin reduced visceral abdominal fat by roughly 15–20% without necessarily producing dramatic changes on the scale.
